author: Claude (EFL materials writer role)
basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate. Claude raised the lexical density on slides 4, 5, 8, 9, 12 and 19, which sat just below the B2 Flesch-Kincaid floor; meaning unchanged.

slides.1: Every international ranking flatters our classrooms, and the device numbers are genuinely impressive. What I want to examine this morning is whether a student in a mountain township sees any of that.
slides.2: Goal four commits us to an education nobody is excluded from, whatever a household earns or wherever it sits on the map. Our semiconductor economy rests on that promise, although its ethics are discussed by almost nobody.
slides.3: Decades of investment in educational hardware produced the prosperity we currently enjoy. With births at a record low and the software rewritten every year, whether that money still lands in the right place has become a fair question.
slides.4: Bandwidth, not talent, determines what a lesson can become. A child in a well-connected district loads a video instantly, whereas a remote school still buffers, and every migration to online teaching widens that distance.
slides.5: What social media cultivates is impatience, not scepticism. Almost nobody has been shown how to trace a claim back to its original source, so a fabricated headline comfortably outruns its correction.
slides.6: Digital safety has quietly turned into a mental-health problem, driven by harassment that follows a teenager home and never switches off. If the school system will not intervene, who exactly is expected to?
slides.7: Look at what the state has actually handed over. Tablets were distributed to thousands of children in rural townships under the "tablets for every student" policy, but a device sitting in a bag teaches nobody anything.
slides.8: The platform side has succeeded beyond anyone's prediction. Courses published free by the government allow a household with no budget for cram school to teach itself programming, which narrows a gap money would otherwise determine.
slides.9: Participation figures here run comfortably beyond the international average, and teachers have been retrained for distance instruction. Numbers of that kind, however, can disguise how insubstantial an hour in front of a screen actually is.
slides.10: Media literacy has finally been written into the syllabus, so a teenager is now taught to interrogate a source before forwarding it. Almost none of the adults in this room were ever given that particular lesson.
slides.11: Over 80% of institutions have adopted digital teaching, and adaptive software now assigns each pupil a different exercise. The processors used in those machines are designed here, though nobody explains who owns the data they collect.
slides.12: Part of the remedy travels by road. Vans equipped as mobile laboratories climb into mountain villages, delivering robotics kits and programming classes to children whose own schools could never finance either.
slides.13: Everything happening in these classrooms sits underneath exports of roughly 500 billion US dollars a year. The same competence will be demanded again when the data is climate data and the deadline is not commercial.
slides.14: Only when the phone is finally put down does the cost become visible: sleep, concentration and ordinary friendship, all of them eroded quietly. Internet addiction among the young is a public-health question, not a personal failing.
slides.15: Ignored for another decade, these structural divisions widen on their own, and a generation of capable people is quietly written off. We are already inside that system, so whether regulation can outrun automation is our question.
slides.16: How well a country resists manipulation is decided long before the manipulation arrives, inside its classrooms. Without sustained reform our advantage in digital innovation will erode, because the syllabus has to keep pace with the tools being sold.
slides.17: Putting the evidence together, we can see genuine advance sitting beside a stubborn problem. We have wired almost every classroom in the country, although a fast line has never by itself produced a fair education.
slides.18: What the rankings actually measure is memory and access, never curiosity. Real reform means changing the incentive so that a student produces something on that screen instead of consuming it for six hours.
slides.19: The next stage must guarantee digital rights for the populations we routinely overlook, and the syllabus requires rebuilding rather than patching. No course should introduce a tool without explaining what that tool does to the person using it.
slides.20: So I am asking something concrete of you. Argue about digital policy wherever it is being decided, teach an older relative to recognize a scam, or sit down beside a teenager and check a claim together.
